decks.title: Rebels and the Raj — Part 1: The Rebellion and Awadh
goals: Describe how the revolt of 1857 began at Meerut and Delhi and spread through cantonments and towns
Explain the common pattern of revolt, the part of rumours and what the evidence for planning can show
Identify the main leaders, their places and their backgrounds
Explain why Awadh became a centre of revolt and read short imagined records on it

slides.heading: Rebels and the Raj
slides.body_md: Part 1: the **rebellion**, its **spread** and **Awadh in revolt**.

visual.alt: Flow chart, Part 1 at a glance: Meerut and Delhi, then Spread and pattern, then Leaders, then Awadh in revolt
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: In 1857 a rising of soldiers became a revolt of many peoples across north India. In this part we follow how it began at Meerut and Delhi, how it spread, who led it, and why Awadh became one of its strongest centres.

slides.heading: From Meerut to Delhi
slides.body_md: On **10 May 1857** sepoys at Meerut mutinied; on **11 May** they reached the Red Fort.

rows: Sepoys at Meerut mutiny after soldiers who had refused the new cartridges are punished
They reach the Red Fort in Delhi; the ageing emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar is asked to lead and agrees
The revolt spreads to Lucknow, Kanpur, Jhansi, Bareilly, Arrah and other places

visual.alt: Table, Meerut to Delhi. 10 May: Sepoys at Meerut mutiny after soldiers who had refused the new cartridges are punished; 11 May: They reach the Red Fort in Delhi; the ageing emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar is asked to lead and agrees; Afterwards: The revolt spreads to Lucknow, Kanpur, Jhansi, Bareilly, Arrah and other places
visual.caption: Meerut to Delhi

slides.narration: On 10 May 1857, sepoys at Meerut mutinied, after soldiers who had refused the new cartridges were punished. They rode to Delhi, and on 11 May reached the Red Fort. There the ageing Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, was asked to be their leader, and he agreed. From there the revolt spread to many cantonments and towns.

slides.heading: Reports and rumours
slides.body_md: Cartridges, flour and chapatis: reports that **alarmed** or **puzzled** people.

rows: New Enfield rifle cartridges said to be greased with cow and pig fat
Contact with the fat would offend many Hindu and Muslim sepoys
Bone dust said to be mixed in flour sold in markets
It seemed a plot against food and faith
Chapatis reported to be passed from village to village
A report of something moving hand to hand between villages

visual.alt: Table, Reports and rumours of 1857. New Enfield rifle cartridges said to be greased with cow and pig fat: Contact with the fat would offend many Hindu and Muslim sepoys; Bone dust said to be mixed in flour sold in markets: It seemed a plot against food and faith; Chapatis reported to be passed from village to village: A report of something moving hand to hand between villages
visual.caption: Reports and rumours of 1857

slides.narration: Rumours were part of the story. People said the cartridges of the new Enfield rifle were greased with the fat of cows and pigs, and that bone dust was mixed into flour sold in markets. Chapatis were reported to be passed from village to village. Each report is something a historian must weigh, not simply accept.

slides.body_md: On which date in 1857 did sepoys at Meerut mutiny?
slides.narration: Recall the date on which the revolt began.

slides.heading: Why rumours spread
slides.body_md: A rumour travels when it **fits a fear** that people already hold.

visual.alt: Flow chart, Why rumours spread: Fears about British intentions, then Reforms, missionaries, annexations, then A rumour fits the fear, then It is believed and repeated
visual.caption: Why rumours spread

slides.narration: Why did such rumours spread? Because they reflected fears about British intentions. Reforms such as the abolition of sati and the permission for widow remarriage, English education, the work of missionaries and the annexation of states had made many people uneasy. A rumour that fitted these fears was easy to believe and easy to repeat.

slides.narration: This timeline places the events from 1856 to 1859. Awadh was annexed in 1856. The sepoys rose at Meerut in May 1857. Delhi was recaptured in September 1857, Lucknow was retaken in March 1858, and the Rani of Jhansi died in June 1858. British rule passed to the Crown in 1858. Two famous British paintings date from 1858 and 1859.

slides.heading: A common pattern
slides.body_md: First the **sepoys**, then the **townspeople and villagers**.

nodes.label: Sepoys seize arms and the treasury
Attack jail, telegraph office, records room

visual.alt: Flow chart, The common pattern: Sepoys seize arms and the treasury, then Attack jail, telegraph office, records room, then Townspeople and villagers join, then Moneylenders and the rich attacked
visual.caption: The common pattern

slides.narration: A common pattern appears in many places. Sepoys seized arms and the treasury, then attacked government buildings such as the jail, the telegraph office and the records room. After that, townspeople and villagers joined in. Many attacked moneylenders and other rich people who were seen as allies of the British.

slides.heading: Was it planned?
slides.body_md: Messages between regiments and night meetings show **contact**; they do not prove a **plan**.

rows: Why historians speak carefully about organisation

visual.alt: Table, Evidence for planning. Messages passed between regiments: Some contact between units; Night meetings of sepoy panchayats: Some discussion among sepoys; The gaps in the records: Why historians speak carefully about organisation
visual.caption: Evidence for planning

slides.narration: Was the revolt planned? Regiments sent messages to one another, and panchayats of sepoys met at night. That suggests some contact and discussion among sepoys. But contact is not the same as a plan, and the records have gaps, so historians speak carefully about how far the revolt was organised.

visual.caption: Reading a magistrate's note

slides.narration: Take an imagined note by a magistrate. It says the sepoys emptied the treasury, and that on the third day villagers burned the revenue registers. The first fact shows the sepoy stage and the second the civilian stage, so the note fits the common pattern. What is missing is who gave the orders and what the villagers wanted.

slides.heading: Leaders of the revolt
slides.body_md: Leaders came from **ruling families**, from **zamindars**, and from **peasant and tribal** communities.

Queen of a state hit by the doctrine of lapse

Nana Sahib: Kanpur: Adopted son of Baji Rao II, the last Peshwa; Rani Lakshmi Bai: Jhansi: Queen of a state hit by the doctrine of lapse; Kunwar Singh: Arrah, Bihar: Zamindar; Begum Hazrat Mahal: Lucknow: Put forward her son Birjis Qadr as nawab; Shah Mal: Baraut region: Peasant leader; Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah: Faizabad: A maulvi; Gonoo: Singhbhum, Chotanagpur: Tribal cultivator
visual.caption: Leaders of the revolt

slides.narration: The revolt had many leaders. Nana Sahib, the adopted son of the last Peshwa, led at Kanpur. Rani Lakshmi Bai led at Jhansi. Kunwar Singh was a zamindar of Arrah. Begum Hazrat Mahal put forward her son at Lucknow. Shah Mal was a peasant leader, and Gonoo a tribal cultivator. Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah was a leader at Faizabad.

slides.heading: How Awadh was lost
slides.body_md: Bound by the **Subsidiary Alliance**, then **annexed in 1856**.

nodes.label: Nawab Wajid Ali Shah exiled to Calcutta

visual.alt: Flow chart, How Awadh was lost: Subsidiary Alliance, Wellesley, 1798, then Annexation for misgovernment, Dalhousie, 1856, then Nawab Wajid Ali Shah exiled to Calcutta, then Court and army dissolved
visual.caption: How Awadh was lost

slides.narration: Awadh had been bound by the Subsidiary Alliance, which Lord Wellesley introduced in 1798. In 1856, Lord Dalhousie annexed it on the ground of misgovernment. The nawab, Wajid Ali Shah, was dethroned and exiled to Calcutta, and his court and army were dissolved.

visual.caption: Why Awadh became a centre of revolt

slides.narration: This diagram shows how the annexation led to several grievances. The court and army were dissolved, taluqdars lost lands in the settlement, and the revenue demand on peasants did not fall much. Because many sepoys came from Awadh villages, these grievances met in the barracks. Together they made Awadh a centre of long resistance.

slides.heading: Taluqdars and peasants
slides.body_md: The **summary settlement of 1856** removed many taluqdars from their lands.

rows: Held forts and had armed retainers

visual.alt: Table, Groups in Awadh. Taluqdars: Held forts and had armed retainers: Many removed from their lands; Peasants: Followed their taluqdars: Revenue demand not much lower; Court servants and soldiers: Served the nawab: Court and army dissolved
visual.caption: Groups in Awadh

slides.narration: Taluqdars were large landholders with forts and armed retainers. The summary settlement of 1856 removed many of them from their lands. The British expected peasants to welcome this. But the revenue demand on peasants did not fall much, and many peasants joined their taluqdars in revolt.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: weighing two explanations
slides.body_md: Imagined village: *peasants rose with their taluqdar.* Was it the **demand** or **loyalty**?
bullets: Step 4 — Say what **cannot yet be said**.

rows: Petitions that mention revenue, against orders from the taluqdar
We cannot say which mattered more

visual.alt: Table, Weighing two explanations. Explanation A: The revenue demand stayed heavy; Explanation B: Loyalty to the taluqdar; What would separate them: Petitions that mention revenue, against orders from the taluqdar; Until then: We cannot say which mattered more
visual.caption: Weighing two explanations

slides.narration: Take an imagined village that rose. One explanation says the revenue demand stayed heavy. Another says peasants were loyal to their taluqdar. To choose between them, a historian looks for petitions that mention revenue and for orders that came from the taluqdar. Until then she cannot say which mattered more.

slides.heading: Sepoys and villages
slides.body_md: Many sepoys came from **Awadh villages**, so grievances were **linked**.

rows: Many sepoys of the Bengal army came from Awadh villages
What troubled the villages was also felt in the barracks
Army and countryside rose together in many places

visual.alt: Table, Sepoys and villages. Recruitment: Many sepoys of the Bengal army came from Awadh villages; Shared grievance: What troubled the villages was also felt in the barracks; Effect: Army and countryside rose together in many places
visual.caption: Sepoys and villages

slides.narration: Many sepoys of the Company's Bengal army came from villages of Awadh. So the grievances of the villages were also felt in the barracks. The link between sepoys and peasants is one reason the resistance there was widespread and lasted so long.

slides.heading: Lucknow
slides.body_md: **Begum Hazrat Mahal** put forward her son **Birjis Qadr** as nawab.

visual.alt: Table, Lucknow. Leader: Begum Hazrat Mahal; Nawab put forward: Her young son Birjis Qadr; Regime: A rebel administration at Lucknow; End: Lucknow finally retaken in March 1858
visual.caption: Lucknow

slides.narration: At Lucknow, Begum Hazrat Mahal put forward her young son, Birjis Qadr, as nawab, and his regime acted as a rebel administration. Awadh saw some of the longest resistance. Lucknow was finally retaken by the British only in March 1858.

bullets: Step 1 — Find a **known event** in each note.
Step 2 — Place each event on the **timeline**.

rows: The emperor sits in the Red Fort
The Meerut sepoys have just risen

rows: 10 May 1857 Meerut; 11 May Delhi; Bahadur Shah Zafar leads

slides.narration: To sum up. The revolt began at Meerut on 10 May 1857, and Bahadur Shah Zafar was asked to lead at Delhi. It spread by a common pattern, with rumours reflecting fears, and with many leaders of different backgrounds. Awadh joined because annexation, the settlement and the link between sepoys and villages produced many grievances.

decks.title: Rebels and the Raj — Part 2: Aims, Repression and Images
goals: Describe what the rebels wanted, from their proclamations, their targets and their administrations
Describe how the British put down the revolt, briefly and neutrally
Interpret British and nationalist images of 1857 as representations made for audiences
Explain why the labels mutiny and first war of independence form a debate about naming

slides.heading: Aims, Repression and Images
slides.body_md: Part 2: **what the rebels wanted**, **repression**, **images** and **naming**.

visual.alt: Flow chart, Part 2 at a glance: What the rebels wanted, then Repression, then Images of the revolt, then Reading visual sources
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In this part we ask what the rebels wanted, how the British put the revolt down, and how it has been pictured since. Pictures are not photographs. They were made by people, for audiences, and they shaped how the revolt was remembered.

slides.heading: What the proclamations said
slides.body_md: Appeals to **all sections** of society, **regardless of religion**.

rows: In the name of Bahadur Shah, and one at Azamgarh in August 1857
Hindus and Muslims together; people of all religions
British rule for its effects on zamindars, merchants, artisans, officials and religious leaders

visual.alt: Table, Rebel proclamations. Issued: In the name of Bahadur Shah, and one at Azamgarh in August 1857; Called on: Hindus and Muslims together; people of all religions; Attacked: British rule for its effects on zamindars, merchants, artisans, officials and religious leaders
visual.caption: Rebel proclamations

slides.narration: Rebel proclamations appealed to all sections of society regardless of religion. One was issued in the name of Bahadur Shah, and another at Azamgarh in August 1857. They called on Hindus and Muslims together to fight, and attacked British rule for its effects on zamindars, merchants, artisans, officials and religious leaders.

slides.heading: Unity and the British attempt
slides.body_md: The attempt to portray the revolt as a **conflict between communities** largely failed in the main centres.

rows: To present the revolt as a conflict between communities
Largely failed in the main centres

visual.alt: Table, Unity and the British attempt. The rebel appeal: Unity across religions; The British attempt: To present the revolt as a conflict between communities; Result: Largely failed in the main centres
visual.caption: Unity and the British attempt

slides.narration: The British tried to present the revolt as a conflict between communities. In the main centres, this attempt largely failed. We describe this neutrally. It is a finding drawn from the records, and it does not rest on praise or blame of any group.

slides.heading: Quick check: proclamations
slides.body_md: Which feature do the rebel proclamations share?
slides.narration: Recall what the proclamations called for.

slides.heading: An earlier world and parallel rule
slides.body_md: Rebels sought to **restore an earlier world** and set up **parallel administrations**.

nodes.label: Hope to restore an earlier world

visual.alt: Flow chart, Restoring and governing: Hope to restore an earlier world, then Look to the Mughal emperor, then Parallel administrations, then Delhi court and Lucknow regime
visual.caption: Restoring and governing

slides.narration: Rebels sought to restore an earlier world, which is why they looked to the authority of the Mughal emperor. Some set up parallel administrations. In Delhi there was a court of administration, and in Lucknow the regime of Birjis Qadr. These show an attempt to govern, and not only to fight.

slides.heading: Who and what was attacked
slides.body_md: **Moneylenders** and the **rich** were seen as allies of the British.

rows: Seen as allies of the British
Many groups, each with its own reasons

visual.alt: Table, Targets of the rebels. Moneylenders and the rich: Seen as allies of the British; Government buildings: Marks of British power; Result: Many groups, each with its own reasons
visual.caption: Targets of the rebels

slides.narration: Rebels also attacked moneylenders and the rich, who were seen as allies of the British. They attacked government buildings too. This shows that the revolt carried the grievances of many groups, and that different groups had their own reasons for taking part.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: reading a rebel notice
slides.body_md: Imagined notice: *speaks to merchants and artisans; calls on Hindus and Muslims to stand together.*

What the authors wished others to believe

visual.caption: Reading a rebel notice

slides.narration: Take an imagined rebel notice of a kind historians study. It speaks to merchants and artisans, and calls on Hindus and Muslims to stand together. It shows what its authors wished others to believe and whom they hoped to win over. What is missing is whether people answered the call.

slides.heading: Repression
slides.body_md: Laws of **May and June 1857** put north India under **martial law**.

nodes.label: Laws of 1857: martial law in north India
Officers and ordinary Britons may try suspects

visual.alt: Flow chart, Steps of repression: Laws of 1857: martial law in north India, then Officers and ordinary Britons may try suspects, then Reinforcements from Britain, then Delhi and Lucknow retaken
visual.caption: Steps of repression

slides.narration: The British acted quickly. From May and June 1857, laws put north India under martial law. Military officers, and even ordinary Britons, could try and punish Indians suspected of rebellion. Reinforcements came from Britain. We state this plainly, without detail, since violence occurred on both sides.

slides.heading: How the revolt ended
slides.body_md: Delhi, Lucknow, Jhansi and the **Crown** in 1858.

rows: Bahadur Shah tried and exiled to Rangoon; died there in 1862
The Rani of Jhansi dies fighting
British rule passes from the Company to the Crown

visual.alt: Table, How the revolt ended. Late September 1857: Delhi recaptured; After the recapture: Bahadur Shah tried and exiled to Rangoon; died there in 1862; March 1858: Lucknow finally retaken; June 1858: The Rani of Jhansi dies fighting; 1858: British rule passes from the Company to the Crown; End of 1858 to 1859: Revolt largely suppressed
visual.caption: How the revolt ended

slides.narration: Delhi was recaptured in late September 1857. Bahadur Shah was tried and exiled to Rangoon, where he died in 1862. Lucknow was finally retaken in March 1858, and the Rani of Jhansi died fighting in June 1858. The revolt was largely suppressed by the end of 1858 or 1859, and British rule passed from the Company to the Crown in 1858.

sections.heading: 1. Meerut, Delhi and the spread
sections.body_md:
On **10 May 1857**, sepoys at **Meerut** mutinied, after soldiers who had refused the new cartridges were punished. They went to Delhi, and on **11 May** reached the **Red Fort**, where the ageing Mughal emperor **Bahadur Shah Zafar** was asked to lead them and agreed. The revolt then spread to cantonments and towns across north India, among them Lucknow, Kanpur, Jhansi, Bareilly and Arrah.

**Reports and rumours** shaped feeling. People said the cartridges of the new Enfield rifle were greased with the fat of cows and pigs, which would offend many Hindu and Muslim soldiers, and that bone dust was mixed into flour sold in markets. Chapatis were reported to be passed from village to village. Such rumours travelled because they matched fears about British intentions: reforms such as the abolition of sati and widow remarriage, English education, the work of missionaries, and annexations.

A report passed on without proof, which may still show what people feared.

sections.heading: 2. The pattern of revolt, planning and leaders
sections.body_md:
In many places a **common pattern** appeared. Sepoys took arms and the treasury and attacked government buildings (the jail, the telegraph office, the records room). The civilian population then joined in, and moneylenders and other rich people, seen as allies of the British, were attacked.

Regiments sent **messages** to one another and **panchayats of sepoys** met at night. This points to some contact and discussion; historians weigh how far it amounts to a plan.

**Leaders** came from many backgrounds: **Nana Sahib**, adopted son of Baji Rao II, the last Peshwa, at Kanpur; **Rani Lakshmi Bai** at Jhansi; **Kunwar Singh**, a zamindar of Arrah in Bihar; **Begum Hazrat Mahal** at Lucknow, who put forward her young son **Birjis Qadr** as nawab; **Shah Mal**, a peasant leader in the Baraut region of Uttar Pradesh; **Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah** of Faizabad; and **Gonoo**, a tribal cultivator of Singhbhum in Chotanagpur.

sections.heading: 3. Awadh in revolt
sections.body_md:
Awadh had been bound by the **Subsidiary Alliance**, introduced by **Lord Wellesley** in 1798. In **1856**, **Lord Dalhousie** annexed it on the ground of misgovernment, dethroned the nawab **Wajid Ali Shah** and exiled him to Calcutta. His court and army were dissolved, leaving many without a living. Dalhousie's **doctrine of lapse**, which annexed states whose rulers died without a natural heir (Jhansi, Satara and Nagpur are examples), is the wider setting; Awadh itself was taken on the other ground.

The **summary settlement of 1856** removed many **taluqdars**, large landholders with forts and armed retainers, from their lands. The British expected peasants to welcome this, but the revenue demand on peasants did not fall much, and many joined their taluqdars. Many sepoys of the Company's **Bengal army** came from Awadh villages, so the grievances of army and countryside were linked. Awadh saw some of the longest resistance, and Lucknow was finally retaken in March 1858.

sections.heading: 4. What the rebels wanted
sections.body_md:
Rebel **proclamations**, such as one issued in the name of Bahadur Shah and one from Azamgarh in August 1857, appealed to all sections of society regardless of religion. They called on Hindus and Muslims together to fight, and criticised British rule for its effects on zamindars, merchants, artisans, officials and religious leaders.

The rebels sought to **restore an earlier world**, looking to the authority of the Mughal emperor. Some set up **parallel administrations**: a court of administration in Delhi and the regime of Birjis Qadr in Lucknow. They attacked moneylenders and the rich, who were seen as allies of the British. The British tried to portray the revolt as a conflict between communities; in the main centres this largely failed. A proclamation shows what its authors hoped for, and it is read with other evidence.

sections.heading: 5. Repression and the end of the revolt
sections.body_md:
From **May and June 1857** the British passed laws that put north India under **martial law** and let military officers, and even ordinary Britons, try and punish Indians suspected of rebellion. **Reinforcements** came from Britain. Violence occurred on both sides, and it is stated here briefly and neutrally.

**Delhi** was recaptured in late September 1857; Bahadur Shah was tried and exiled to **Rangoon**, where he died in 1862. **Lucknow** was finally retaken in March 1858, and the **Rani of Jhansi** died fighting in June 1858. The revolt was largely suppressed by the end of 1858 or 1859, and in 1858 British rule passed from the Company to the **Crown**.

key_terms.definition_md: Rule by military authority, with trial and punishment by officers.
The British monarchy, which took over rule from the Company in 1858.

sections.heading: 6. Images of the revolt
sections.body_md:
Pictures were **made by people for audiences** and shaped memory; historians read them as **representations**. Many **British** pictures and cartoons showed the British as heroic rescuers and as avenging justice, and the rebels as violent. **Thomas Jones Barker** painted the relief of Lucknow (1859), with Colin Campbell, James Outram and Henry Havelock; **Joseph Noel Paton** painted In Memoriam (1858) about English women and children. Cartoons in the London magazine **Punch** commented on Governor-General **Canning's** call for moderation; critics nicknamed him **Clemency Canning**.

In the twentieth century **nationalist** images celebrated the Rani of Jhansi and others as heroes. **V. D. Savarkar** called the revolt the first war of Indian independence in 1909. The names **mutiny** and **first war of independence** each carry a view; historians treat them as a debate about naming.

key_terms.definition_md: A picture or account made by someone for an audience, and not a direct record of events.
The nickname given by critics to Governor-General Canning for his call for moderation.

sections.heading: 7. Sources: reading visual representations
sections.body_md:
To read a picture, ask five questions: **what** is shown, **how** (size, colour, position, what is small and what is central), **who** made it, **for whom** and **when**. Then ask what it cannot tell. A picture made by someone who was not there is evidence of what its makers and buyers imagined, and not a witness of the scene.

Use pictures with other sources, such as diaries, letters and official records, which may show a different view. In SOYL practice, the pictures in source questions are **imagined** and described in words; the board paper will give its own.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing the revolt as one planned conspiracy; say some contact, with causes in many places.
- Naming leaders without their places and backgrounds.
- Saying peasants welcomed the end of taluqdari; the demand did not fall much.
- Confusing the Subsidiary Alliance (Wellesley, 1798) with the annexation of Awadh (Dalhousie, 1856).
- Treating a painting or cartoon as a photograph of events.
- Presenting mutiny or first war of independence as the only right label; it is a debate.
- Blaming a community, or adding detail of violence; be neutral and brief.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: one correct option.
- 2 marks: two points, or a point and a reason (30–50 words).
- 3 marks: three distinct points (50–80 words).
- 5 marks: five headed points (80–120 words); assess questions need more than one side and a judgement.
- Source questions (4 marks): parts (a) and (b) one mark each, part (c) two marks with an internal choice.

**Sources in SOYL practice** are imagined documents, imagined descriptions of imagined pictures, or SOYL summaries written for practice.

cards.back_md: At Meerut, on 10 May 1857, when sepoys mutinied after soldiers who had refused the new cartridges were punished.

questions.stem_md: On which date in 1857 did the sepoys at Meerut mutiny, starting the revolt?

options.text_md: 11 May
10 May
29 March
20 June

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 10 May. The Meerut sepoys rose on 10 May; on the following day they reached Delhi.

questions.stem_md: Historians argue that rumours travelled fast in 1857 when they matched what people already feared about the intentions of the British. Which of these imagined rumours, circulating in a north Indian cantonment and its villages, would on that reasoning have spread fastest?

options.text_md: That the monsoon of the coming year would arrive earlier than usual
That a new parade ground would be laid out beside the cantonment
That the price of salt would be fixed by a new committee
That the government meant to undermine the faith of the people by mixing forbidden substances into food and by sending missionaries

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** That the government meant to undermine the faith of the people by mixing forbidden substances into food and by sending missionaries. Only the first rumour touches the fears of interference with religion and custom that people already held about the new rulers. The others concern weather, buildings or prices, which carry no such charge.

questions.stem_md: Why did the report that the new Enfield rifle cartridges were greased with animal fat alarm sepoys of both Hindu and Muslim faiths?

options.text_md: The fat was said to come from cows and pigs, and contact with it would offend the religious feelings of many soldiers of both faiths
The cartridges were said to be too heavy to carry on long marches
The cost of the cartridges was to be taken out of the sepoys' pay
The cartridges were said to be meant only for British regiments

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The fat was said to come from cows and pigs, and contact with it would offend the religious feelings of many soldiers of both faiths. The rumoured fat of cows and pigs touched the religious sentiments of Hindu and Muslim soldiers alike. The other reports are not part of the cartridge rumour.

questions.stem_md: Historians describe a common pattern: sepoys seize arms and the treasury and attack government buildings, and then townspeople and villagers join in, often attacking moneylenders. Three imagined towns are reported. In town P the sepoys took the treasury and opened the jail, and the next day a crowd looted a moneylender's house. In town Q a crowd from nearby villages attacked a moneylender and a revenue office, and no soldiers took part. In town R the sepoys took arms and the treasury, then marched away to join others, and no civilians acted. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: All three towns follow the whole pattern
Only R follows the pattern, because the sepoys acted first
P follows the whole pattern, while Q and R each follow only part of it
Q follows the whole pattern, because a moneylender was attacked

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** P follows the whole pattern, while Q and R each follow only part of it. Check each town against both stages. P has the sepoy stage and the civilian stage. Q lacks the sepoy stage and R lacks the civilian stage.

questions.stem_md: Some historians think the revolt was not wholly spontaneous, because regiments sent messages to one another and sepoy panchayats met at night. Which finding about an imagined cantonment would most weaken this view?

options.text_md: The messages were carried by sepoys who travelled between stations on foot
The night meetings were held in the week before the regiment rose
The surviving messages between its regiments concern only leave, pay and a quarrel over rations, and the night meetings dealt with nothing else
Several regiments in neighbouring stations rose within days of one another

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The surviving messages between its regiments concern only leave, pay and a quarrel over rations, and the night meetings dealt with nothing else. The inference of planning rests on the content of the contacts. If they were about ordinary regimental matters, the contacts no longer point to a plan. The other findings are consistent with planning or neutral.

questions.stem_md: Which pair of leaders of 1857 came from peasant or tribal backgrounds, and not from ruling or landed families?

options.text_md: Shah Mal of the Baraut region and Gonoo of Singhbhum
Nana Sahib and Begum Hazrat Mahal
Kunwar Singh and Rani Lakshmi Bai
Begum Hazrat Mahal and Kunwar Singh

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Shah Mal of the Baraut region and Gonoo of Singhbhum. Shah Mal was a peasant leader and Gonoo a tribal cultivator. The other pairs include a Peshwa's adopted son, a begum, a queen and a zamindar.

questions.stem_md: An imagined undated letter by a clerk in a north Indian town says that the old emperor sits in the Red Fort, that rebel soldiers hold Delhi, and that the Company's reinforcements have not yet reached the city. Within which period was it most probably written?

options.text_md: Before 10 May 1857, since the sepoys had not yet risen
After the final retaking of Lucknow in March 1858
In 1862, when the old emperor died in exile
Between 11 May 1857 and the recapture of Delhi in late September 1857

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Between 11 May 1857 and the recapture of Delhi in late September 1857. The emperor in the Red Fort at the head of the rebels puts the letter after 11 May 1857, and rebel control of Delhi puts it before the city was recaptured. The other dates contradict one of these clues.

questions.stem_md: In many places rebel sepoys, after taking arms and the treasury, attacked the jail, the telegraph office and the records room. Which explanation fits all three targets best?

options.text_md: All three were the richest buildings of a cantonment, so the aim was only plunder
Each stood for a power of the government: to hold prisoners, to send orders and news quickly, and to keep records of dues and decisions
All three were used only by Indian clerks, whom the sepoys wished to punish
All three housed the families of British officers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Each stood for a power of the government: to hold prisoners, to send orders and news quickly, and to keep records of dues and decisions. The common feature of the three targets is administrative power. The other explanations do not fit all three: a jail or a records room holds no wealth, and none of them was a family residence.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Kunwar Singh, a leader of the revolt, was a zamindar of Arrah in Bihar.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** He is remembered as the zamindar of Arrah who took up arms.

questions.stem_md: At Delhi the sepoys asked the ageing Mughal emperor ___ to be their leader, and he agreed.
questions.solution_md: Bahadur Shah Zafar accepted the leadership on 11 May 1857.

questions.stem_md: Match each leader of 1857 with the place where he or she is chiefly remembered.

options.text_md: Nana Sahib
Rani Lakshmi Bai
Kunwar Singh
Begum Hazrat Mahal

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Nana Sahib was the adopted son of Baji Rao II, the last Peshwa. Begum Hazrat Mahal put forward her son as nawab.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined station records of 1857. At station X, sepoys rose on 20 May and a bazaar crowd attacked a moneylender on 21 May. At station Y, villagers burned a moneylender's account books on 18 May and the sepoys rose on 22 May. Which station follows the usual order of events, and what does the other record suggest?
questions.solution_md: Station X fits the order of the two stages; the reversed order at Y points to an independent village grievance.

answer.model_answer_md: **Station X** follows the usual order, with the sepoys first and civilians afterwards. At **station Y** the villagers acted four days before the sepoys, which suggests that **local grievances against moneylenders** moved them on their own, and that the sepoys did not set them going.

marking_scheme.step: X identified as following the usual order
Y's reversed order read as a local grievance

questions.stem_md: A source reports that chapatis were passed from village to village in 1857. State one thing a historian could reasonably infer from this report and one thing that the report alone cannot tell her.
questions.solution_md: A cautious inference and a stated limit.

answer.model_answer_md: She can infer that **something was being passed by hand between villages**, so news or alarm could travel quickly along village links. The report alone cannot tell her **what the chapatis meant** to those who passed them on, or whether anyone organised the practice.

marking_scheme.step: A limit: meaning or organiser unknown

questions.stem_md: Why did rumours about the cartridges and about bone dust in flour spread so quickly in 1857?
questions.solution_md: The fit between rumour and fear is the cause of the quick spread.

answer.model_answer_md: They fitted **existing fears about British intentions**, such as interference with religion and custom. People already uneasy about reforms, missionary activity and annexations were **ready to believe** a report that matched those fears, and so they repeated it.

marking_scheme.step: The rumours matched fears about British intentions
Link with reforms, missionaries or annexations

questions.stem_md: Compare Nana Sahib and Shah Mal as leaders of 1857, naming where each acted and his background, and say what the difference suggests about the revolt.
questions.solution_md: Two leaders placed and described, and an inference about the breadth of leadership.

answer.model_answer_md: **Nana Sahib**, the adopted son of Baji Rao II, the last Peshwa, led at **Kanpur** and could draw on a ruling family's name. **Shah Mal** was a **peasant leader** in the Baraut region of Uttar Pradesh. The difference suggests that the revolt drew leaders from **ruling families and from ordinary villagers**, so it was not the work of one class.

questions.stem_md: To what extent was the spread of the revolt of 1857 planned, and to what extent did it arise from circumstances? Use the evidence of the pattern of revolt, the messages between regiments and the rumours.
questions.solution_md: Evidence for planning, evidence for circumstances, the part of rumours and of civilians, and a measured judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **For planning:** sepoys sent messages between regiments and sepoy panchayats met at night, which suggests some coordination.
2. **For circumstances:** the revolt began at Meerut after soldiers who refused the new cartridges were punished, and it spread as others learnt that Delhi had a leader.
3. **Rumours** about cartridges and flour passed quickly because they matched fears about British intentions, which made many ready to act.
4. **Civilians** joined after the sepoys had risen and attacked moneylenders, which looks like local grievance and not a single plan.
5. **Judgement:** some planning among sepoys is likely, but the wide spread owed more to shared fears and local causes.

questions.stem_md: Which Governor-General annexed Awadh in 1856 on the ground that its nawab had misgoverned?

options.text_md: Lord Dalhousie
Lord Wellesley
Lord Canning
Lord Cornwallis

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Lord Dalhousie. Dalhousie annexed Awadh and the nawab, Wajid Ali Shah, was sent to Calcutta. Wellesley is linked with the Subsidiary Alliance and Canning was Governor-General during the revolt.

questions.stem_md: Whom did Begum Hazrat Mahal put forward as the nawab during the revolt at Lucknow?

options.text_md: The dethroned Wajid Ali Shah
Her young son Birjis Qadr
Nana Sahib
Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Her young son Birjis Qadr. Her son Birjis Qadr was set up as nawab, and his regime acted as a rebel administration in Lucknow.

questions.stem_md: Historians explain that many peasants of Awadh joined their taluqdars in the revolt partly because the revenue demand on peasants did not fall much once the taluqdars were removed. Which finding about an imagined district would most weaken this explanation?

options.text_md: Records showing that the demand stayed the same and that peasants rose with their taluqdars
Petitions from peasants asking that the taluqdars be restored
Records showing that the demand on peasants fell sharply there, yet peasants rose with their taluqdars in equal numbers
Records showing that taluqdars had lent grain to peasants in a bad year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Records showing that the demand on peasants fell sharply there, yet peasants rose with their taluqdars in equal numbers. An explanation is weakened when the effect appears even though the supposed cause is absent. The other findings are consistent with the explanation or point to other ties.

questions.stem_md: Which imagined finding would best support the claim that the grievances of sepoys and of peasants were linked in Awadh?

options.text_md: Pay registers showing that the sepoys were paid on time
Recruitment lists showing that no sepoys came from Awadh villages
Records of a regiment recruited wholly from another region
Letters from sepoys that discuss the village revenue demand, and village petitions that mention sons serving in the Company's army

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Letters from sepoys that discuss the village revenue demand, and village petitions that mention sons serving in the Company's army. A link needs evidence that the two groups shared concerns and were connected by families. Only the first finding shows both.

questions.stem_md: Which of these imagined persons of Lucknow would historians be LEAST likely to find among those who lost out because of the annexation of Awadh?

options.text_md: A retainer of a taluqdar whose fort and lands were taken in the settlement
A courtier whose place vanished when the nawab's court was dissolved
A soldier of the nawab's army who lost his post
A Company official who gained a post in the new administration

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A Company official who gained a post in the new administration. The annexation brought new posts for the Company's servants. The other three lost land, place or employment.

questions.stem_md: Dalhousie's doctrine of lapse allowed the annexation of a state whose ruler died without a natural heir. An imagined state loses its raja, who leaves only an adopted son; a second imagined state loses its raja, who leaves a son by birth. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: The doctrine could be applied only to the second state; and Awadh was annexed for the same reason as the first
The doctrine could be applied to both states, and Awadh was annexed by it
The doctrine could be applied only to the first state; and Awadh, unlike it, was annexed on the ground of misgovernment
The doctrine could be applied to neither state, since lapse applied only to Awadh

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The doctrine could be applied only to the first state; and Awadh, unlike it, was annexed on the ground of misgovernment. Apply the criterion of a missing natural heir to each state. Jhansi, Satara and Nagpur are examples of lapse, while the ground given for Awadh was misgovernment.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Awadh had earlier been bound by the Subsidiary Alliance.

**Reason (R):** The Subsidiary Alliance was introduced by Lord Dalhousie in 1798.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Awadh was indeed bound by the alliance, but it was Lord Wellesley who introduced it in 1798. Dalhousie came later.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Many sepoys of the Company's Bengal army came from villages of Awadh.

**Reason (R):** Awadh was annexed in 1856 on the ground of misgovernment.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are accurate, but the annexation did not cause the army's recruitment from Awadh villages; it only gave those sepoys a fresh grievance later.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Awadh saw some of the longest resistance during the revolt.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Resistance in Awadh continued well after Delhi was recaptured; Lucknow was finally retaken only in March 1858.

questions.stem_md: In Awadh, the large landholders who had forts and armed retainers were called ___.
questions.solution_md: Taluqdars lost lands under the settlement of 1856; many peasants and retainers followed them.

questions.stem_md: A student writes: Awadh rose in 1857 because the British raised the tax on peasants far above what the taluqdars had taken, so the peasants alone made the revolt. Say what is wrong or only partly right in this claim, and correct it.
questions.solution_md: The peasants' part is accepted, the claim about a sharp rise is corrected, and the other groups are added.

answer.model_answer_md: The claim is **partly right**: peasants did join the revolt, and their burden was a grievance. But the demand on them **did not rise sharply; it failed to fall** as the British had expected. Nor did peasants act alone: **taluqdars, dismissed court servants and soldiers, and sepoys from the villages** also took part.

marking_scheme.step: The demand did not rise sharply but failed to fall

questions.stem_md: In an imagined Awadh district, peasants paid 100 rupees a year in revenue and dues through a taluqdar's agents before 1856, and 97 rupees to the new government's collectors after the settlement. The district officer expects peasants to welcome the change. Explain why many might still join the taluqdar.
questions.solution_md: The small fall in the demand, and the older ties to the taluqdar.

answer.model_answer_md: A fall of three rupees in a hundred was **slight**, so the peasants gained almost nothing from the taluqdar's removal. They also had **ties of loyalty** to him and may have distrusted the new collectors. Their main grievance, the heavy demand, was not met, so they sided with him.

marking_scheme.step: The fall was too small to matter
Ties to the taluqdar or distrust of the new collectors

questions.stem_md: An imagined return gives, for two regiments of the Company's Bengal army, the number of sepoys and how many came from villages of Awadh: Regiment A, 600 of 800; Regiment B, 270 of 900. Work out each share, say whose sepoys were more likely to share the grievances of Awadh's villages, and give one limit of this conclusion.
questions.solution_md: Two shares computed, the regiment named with a reason, and a limit stated.

answer.model_answer_md: **Shares:** A, 600 of 800 is 75 per cent; B, 270 of 900 is 30 per cent. **Regiment A** was more likely to share village grievances, since three in four of its men had homes in Awadh villages. **Limit:** where a sepoy came from does not show what he felt; letters or petitions would be needed.

marking_scheme.step: Regiment A named with a reason

questions.stem_md: Assess how far the removal of the taluqdars explains the long resistance in Awadh. Use evidence about peasants, sepoys and the nawab's court.
questions.solution_md: Taluqdars, peasants, sepoys and the court weighed in turn, with a judgement on how far one cause explains.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Taluqdars:** the summary settlement of 1856 removed many from their lands. They had forts and armed retainers, so they had both reason and means to resist.
2. **Peasants:** the revenue demand did not fall much, so peasants had a grievance of their own and often followed their taluqdars.
3. **Sepoys:** many came from Awadh villages, so the grievances of the army and the countryside were linked.
4. **The court:** the dissolution of the nawab's court and army left many without work.
5. **Judgement:** the taluqdars were central, but the resistance lasted because several groups with separate grievances joined; the settlement alone does not explain it.

marking_scheme.step: A reasoned judgement on how far

questions.stem_md: To which city was Bahadur Shah Zafar exiled after his trial following the recapture of Delhi?

options.text_md: Calcutta
Rangoon
Lucknow
Kanpur

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Rangoon. He died in exile at Rangoon in 1862. Calcutta is where the dethroned nawab of Awadh was sent.

questions.stem_md: Which feature do the rebel proclamations of 1857, such as those issued in the name of Bahadur Shah and at Azamgarh, share?

options.text_md: They called on people of all religions, above all Hindus and Muslims together, to fight British rule
They asked only Muslim soldiers to rise
They asked people to pay revenue to the British until the end of the year
They demanded a republic with an elected assembly

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** They called on people of all religions, above all Hindus and Muslims together, to fight British rule. The proclamations were addressed to all sections of society. The other statements describe aims that the proclamations did not state.

questions.stem_md: Which question could a historian answer best from an imagined proclamation issued in the name of a rebel authority?

options.text_md: How many people in each village actually obeyed it?
How did the rebel leadership want its cause to appear, and whom did it hope to win over?
What price did a peasant pay for grain in that year?
Which regiment was the first to reach the town?

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** How did the rebel leadership want its cause to appear, and whom did it hope to win over? A proclamation records the intentions and appeals of its authors. It says nothing reliable about obedience, prices or troop movements, which need other records.

questions.stem_md: Historians note that British attempts to present the revolt as a conflict between communities largely failed in the main centres. Which finding about an imagined main centre would most weaken this claim?

options.text_md: Proclamations there that were addressed to Hindus and Muslims together
A British report that expected the rebels to divide
Records of a Hindu leader and a Muslim leader acting together
Records showing that its rebel forces split along religious lines and fought each other for weeks

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Records showing that its rebel forces split along religious lines and fought each other for weeks. Only a real, lasting division among the rebels would undermine the claim. The other findings show unity or merely a British expectation.

questions.stem_md: Two historians explain why rebels attacked moneylenders. X says they were seen as allies of the British. Y says they were attacked simply as creditors. Which imagined finding would favour X over Y?

options.text_md: Moneylenders with links to British officials were attacked far more often than those without, although both lent on similar terms
Most attacks came just after the harvest, when debts fell due
Moneylenders of every kind were attacked equally, whatever their links with officials
Debt papers were burnt in the houses that were attacked

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Moneylenders with links to British officials were attacked far more often than those without, although both lent on similar terms. To favour X the finding must separate links with the British from the fact of lending. Only the first does; the others fit Y at least as well.

questions.stem_md: Which finding about an imagined city in 1857 would best show that the rebels had set up a parallel administration, and not merely held the city by force?

options.text_md: A note that rebel soldiers camped in the main square
A list of arms taken from the arsenal
A register of orders issued by a rebel court of administration, dealing with appeals, supplies and the pay of soldiers
A letter praising the courage of the sepoys

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A register of orders issued by a rebel court of administration, dealing with appeals, supplies and the pay of soldiers. A parallel administration shows itself in a continuing system of orders and duties. The other findings describe occupation, seizure or praise.

questions.stem_md: What was the effect of the laws that the British passed in May and June 1857?

options.text_md: Only Indian judges were permitted to try suspected rebels
The annexation of Indian states was ended
Much of north India came under martial law, and military officers and even ordinary Britons could try and punish Indians suspected of rebellion
All rebels were promised a pardon if they gave up their arms within a month

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Much of north India came under martial law, and military officers and even ordinary Britons could try and punish Indians suspected of rebellion. The laws widened the power to try and punish. They did not limit the trials to Indian judges, end annexation or offer a general pardon.

**Reason (R):** The proclamation appealed to people of different religions to fight together.

Choose the correct option.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but the arrival of reinforcements does not account for the content of the laws, which widened who could try suspects.

Choose the correct option.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A rumour of 1857 that bone dust had been mixed into flour sold in markets is useful evidence of the fears of the people who repeated it.

**Reason (R):** A rumour can be valuable to a historian even when it is not true.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A rumour is evidence of what people feared and believed, not of what happened, so its falseness does not remove its value; R gives the reason for A.

questions.stem_md: True or false? After the revolt, British rule in India passed from the East India Company to the Crown in 1858.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Rule passed from the Company to the Crown in 1858.

questions.stem_md: Put these four events of the revolt in the order in which they occurred, earliest first.

options.text_md: The Rani of Jhansi dies fighting (June 1858)
Sepoys rise at Meerut (10 May 1857)
Lucknow is finally retaken (March 1858)
Delhi is recaptured by the British (late September 1857)

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (d) → (c) → (a). The rising at Meerut came first, then the fall of Delhi that year, and the events of 1858 follow in the order March, June.

questions.stem_md: A historian claims that the proclamations issued in the name of Bahadur Shah show that Hindus and Muslims in the rebel camp at Delhi had in fact come together. Name one imagined finding that would strengthen this claim and one that would weaken it.
questions.solution_md: One finding for each direction, resting on how people actually acted.

answer.model_answer_md: **Strengthen:** records that people of both faiths served together in the rebel court of administration and forces, taking orders from one authority. **Weaken:** records that the two groups kept separate camps, quarrelled over command or issued rival orders. A proclamation states a call; only such records show how people acted.

questions.stem_md: An imagined British civilian with no military rank, in a north Indian town in mid 1857, is allowed to try an Indian suspected of rebellion. Which feature of the laws of 1857 does this show, and what might it mean for the suspect?
questions.solution_md: The feature of the laws identified and a reasoned consequence.

answer.model_answer_md: It shows the laws of May to June 1857, which put north India under martial law and let military officers and **even ordinary Britons** try and punish suspects. For the suspect it could mean a **hurried trial by someone with no judicial training**, with little protection against a harsh sentence.

marking_scheme.step: Feature: ordinary Britons allowed to try suspects
A reasoned consequence for the suspect

questions.stem_md: Two imagined notices of 1857 survive from one town. Notice X calls on Hindus and Muslims together to fight. Notice Y, put up by a village group, tells villagers to attack a moneylender and his records. Do they contradict each other? What do they show together about what the rebels wanted?
questions.solution_md: No contradiction, the aim of each notice, and the combined reading.

answer.model_answer_md: They do **not contradict** each other, since they address different audiences and aims. X shows a wish for **unity across religions** against British rule; Y shows a **local grievance** against a moneylender seen as an ally of the British. Together they suggest a common cause joined to varied local aims, so no single notice states what all rebels wanted.

questions.stem_md: Describe three steps by which the British put down the revolt.
questions.solution_md: Laws, reinforcements and the recapture of the main centres.

answer.model_answer_md: They passed **laws in May and June 1857** that put north India under martial law and let military officers and even ordinary Britons try suspects, and **reinforcements** came from Britain. They **recaptured Delhi** in late September 1857 and finally **retook Lucknow** in March 1858. By the end of 1858 to 1859 the revolt had largely been suppressed.

questions.stem_md: Assess the view that the rebels of 1857 were united by a common vision. Support your answer with evidence on both sides.
questions.solution_md: Evidence for a common vision, evidence against, and a balanced conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **For unity:** proclamations issued in Bahadur Shah's name and at Azamgarh appealed to all sections and to Hindus and Muslims together.
2. **For unity:** the rebels looked to the Mughal emperor, hoping to restore an earlier world, and set up parallel administrations in Delhi and Lucknow.
3. **Against:** local groups attacked moneylenders and the rich, so aims varied from place to place; a proclamation records what leaders wished to say.
4. **The British** tried to present the revolt as a conflict between communities, but largely failed in the main centres.
5. **Judgement:** there was a shared hostility to British rule and a call for unity, but no single programme.

marking_scheme.step: Proclamations and the call for unity
The failed British attempt to divide

questions.stem_md: Assess how far the laws of 1857 and the arrival of reinforcements explain how the British regained control of north India by 1859. Weigh them against other evidence about the revolt.
questions.solution_md: Laws, reinforcements, the main centres and rebel weaknesses weighed, with a judgement on how far the first two explain.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **The laws** of May and June 1857 put north India under martial law and let officers and ordinary Britons try suspects, so punishment could be quick and widespread.
2. **Reinforcements** from Britain gave the British the strength to retake Delhi in September 1857 and Lucknow in March 1858.
3. **The main centres** mattered: once the court of administration at Delhi and the regime at Lucknow fell, the rebels lost their rallying points.
4. **Rebel weaknesses:** aims varied by place, with no single programme, which limited common action.
5. **Judgement:** laws and reinforcements were necessary but not enough alone; the loss of the centres and the rebels' scattered aims also explain the outcome.

marking_scheme.step: The loss of the main centres
A reasoned judgement on how far

questions.stem_md: Joseph Noel Paton's painting In Memoriam (1858) was about which subject?

options.text_md: English women and children in the revolt
The last battle of the Rani of Jhansi
The trial of Bahadur Shah Zafar
The recapture of Delhi

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** English women and children in the revolt. The painting concerns English women and children. It is a British image, not a nationalist one.

questions.stem_md: Which theme was common in many British pictures of the revolt made after 1857?

options.text_md: The rebels as heroes of a struggle for freedom
Village life in the months before the revolt
A calm survey of the causes of the revolt
The British as heroic rescuers and bringers of justice, and the rebels as violent

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The British as heroic rescuers and bringers of justice, and the rebels as violent. Rescue and avenging justice were favourite themes of British images. The heroic view of the rebels belongs to later nationalist pictures.

questions.stem_md: Thomas Jones Barker's painting of 1859 on the relief of Lucknow shows Colin Campbell, James Outram and Henry Havelock. What kind of memory of the revolt did such a painting help to build among British viewers?

options.text_md: A memory of the revolt as a rising of the Indian peasantry
A memory of the revolt as a story of British courage and rescue
A memory of the revolt as a failure of the British army
A memory of the revolt as a quarrel among Indian rulers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A memory of the revolt as a story of British courage and rescue. The painting honours British commanders as rescuers. Such pictures made for a British audience shaped a memory centred on British heroism.

questions.stem_md: An imagined cartoon in a London magazine of 1857 shows a small figure named Canning being pushed aside by a crowd of angry soldiers and civilians. Which is the soundest inference?

options.text_md: British opinion was divided over how severely to punish rebels, and the cartoonist sided with those who wanted harsher measures
All British people wanted harsh punishment of the rebels
Canning was dismissed from his office in the same year
The cartoon is an accurate record of a real crowd

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** British opinion was divided over how severely to punish rebels, and the cartoonist sided with those who wanted harsher measures. Critics called for harshness and the cartoon belongs to that argument; a single cartoon reveals one side of a debate and one cartoonist's view, not the opinion of all, nor an event.

questions.stem_md: A historian wants to test the claim that nationalist pictures of the Rani of Jhansi reflect the concerns of the time in which they were made more than the events of 1858. Which imagined finding would best support the claim?

options.text_md: Pictures of her were made on paper of the same size throughout the century
Pictures of her appeared in the greatest numbers in years of nationalist campaigns, and each period stressed different qualities in her
Every picture of her showed the same fort in the background
Pictures of her were first sold in the same town where she died

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Pictures of her appeared in the greatest numbers in years of nationalist campaigns, and each period stressed different qualities in her. The claim concerns the link between a picture and its own period. Only the first finding ties the pictures to changing concerns; the others are physical or local details that say nothing about that link.

questions.stem_md: How should a student describe the labels mutiny and first war of independence for the events of 1857?

options.text_md: As two names for the same view, differing only in their words
As a correct name and a wrong name, settled by the evidence
As two names that reflect different views of the events, which writers still debate
As names that were both first used by the rebels in their proclamations

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** As two names that reflect different views of the events, which writers still debate. Each label carries a view of what the events were. The disagreement is a debate about naming and interpretation, which the evidence alone does not settle.

questions.stem_md: A historian says the word mutiny fits events only where soldiers rose against their officers. Which imagined finding about a district would most clearly show that the word does not describe all that happened there?

options.text_md: Records that a regiment disobeyed its orders
Records that sepoys seized the treasury
Records that some British officers were replaced
Records that peasants, artisans and zamindars took up arms and set up their own authority after the sepoys had gone

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Records that peasants, artisans and zamindars took up arms and set up their own authority after the sepoys had gone. The test is whether people other than soldiers acted on their own account. Only the first finding shows that. The others describe military action.

questions.stem_md: An imagined print published in London in 1860 carries a caption saying that it shows a scene of 1857. Its artist, as his biography shows, never travelled to India. For which purpose is the print most useful to a historian?

options.text_md: Counting how many Indians took part at the scene
Establishing the exact layout of the place in 1857
Showing what the rebels themselves wished to say
Studying how British artists and buyers of 1860 imagined the revolt

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Studying how British artists and buyers of 1860 imagined the revolt. An artist who was not there cannot be a witness of the scene; but the print is solid evidence of what its makers and buyers in 1860 imagined and wished to see.

questions.stem_md: A historian asks how British residents of a north Indian city felt as news of the revolt reached them. Which imagined source is most useful?

options.text_md: A painting made twenty years later for an exhibition in London
A school textbook of the 1930s
Private letters and diaries written by British residents at the time
A nationalist poster of the 1940s

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Private letters and diaries written by British residents at the time. The question concerns feelings at a particular time, so evidence written then by those involved is best. Later images and books tell more about their own periods.

options.text_md: True

questions.solution_md: Varied memory and the makers' own purposes.

answer.model_answer_md: She was **remembered in more than one way**, so there was no single fixed picture. Different makers chose different qualities to admire, such as courage or sorrow, to suit **their own audiences and purposes**, so the posters tell us about the 1930s as much as about 1858.

questions.solution_md: Each source given its own use, and the method for a difference.

answer.model_answer_md: She can use the **diary** for what one witness noticed day by day, and the **painting** for how the British later wished the siege to be remembered. Where they differ she should ask who made each, for whom and why, and not assume that either gives the whole truth.

questions.stem_md: An imagined print sold in London in 1858 shows an officer on horseback with a raised sword, women and children sheltering behind him, and a few small dark figures with weapons running away in the background. State what the print shows about its maker's view, for whom it was probably made, and one thing it cannot tell us.
questions.solution_md: The maker's view, the audience and a limit of the evidence.

answer.model_answer_md: The print shows the British as **protectors and avengers** and the rebels as small and threatening, so the maker's view favoured the British. It was probably made for **British buyers at home** who wanted reassurance and pride. It **cannot tell us** what actually happened at any place, or how Indians saw the events.

questions.stem_md: Explain why the labels mutiny and first war of independence are treated as a debate about naming, and mention one kind of evidence each side would stress.
questions.solution_md: Two labels, two views and the evidence each would stress.

answer.model_answer_md: Each label carries a **view of the events**. Mutiny stresses a **soldiers' revolt** against officers, the picture favoured in British accounts; first war of independence, used by Savarkar in 1909, stresses **wide participation and the aim of ending British rule**. The first side would stress the cartridge dispute and army discontent, the second the part of peasants, rulers and others.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined pictures survive: a print of 1858 sold in London showing British soldiers rescuing women and children, and a poster of the 1930s showing the Rani of Jhansi as a heroine. Assess how far each can be used as evidence about the revolt of 1857.
questions.solution_md: The print and the poster each weighed for memory and for events, and a joint judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **The print** was made soon after the events for British buyers, so it is good evidence of how the British wished to see the revolt, as rescue and justice.
2. It is poor evidence of events, since rebels appear only as threats.
3. **The poster** was made long after, for a nationalist audience, so it shows how later Indians remembered 1857 as a heroic struggle.
4. It too cannot show what happened in 1858.
5. **Judgement:** both are representations; each is strong evidence of the memory of its own time and weak evidence of the events, and diaries and official records are needed to test them.

marking_scheme.step: The print as evidence of British views
The poster as evidence of later memory

questions.stem_md: The events of 1857 are better called a mutiny than a first war of independence. To what extent do you agree? Weigh evidence on both sides.
questions.solution_md: Evidence for and against each label and a balanced judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **For mutiny:** the revolt began among sepoys at Meerut after soldiers who refused the new cartridges were punished, and army discontent was central.
2. **Against:** it spread to towns and villages, where civilians, including peasants, attacked moneylenders and others, and rulers and zamindars led.
3. **For independence:** proclamations called Hindus and Muslims together to fight British rule, and Savarkar so named it in 1909.
4. **Against:** aims differed from place to place, and the nationalist label was applied later.
5. **Judgement:** neither label alone fits; the revolt began as a soldiers' rising but widened, and the names reflect the views of those who coined them.

answer.model_answer_md: It reached **many ordinary British people** at home, so it helped spread a **one-sided memory** of the revolt as British rescue and justice.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Name two things the print can tell a historian about Britain in 1858, and one thing it cannot tell about India in 1857.
children.solution_md: Two uses for British attitudes and a limit for events in India.

answer.model_answer_md: It can tell her **what British makers chose to show** (rescue, justice) and **what buyers were willing to hang at home**. It cannot tell her **what actually happened** at any place in India, or how Indians saw it.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Suppose another print of 1858 shows the same scene with the rebels drawn large and the officer small. Explain what kind of maker, audience or purpose might lie behind such a different picture.
alternatives.solution_md: A different purpose or audience that explains a different picture.

answer.model_answer_md: Such a print might come from a **maker who wished to criticise the way the revolt was handled** or to stress the **danger the rebels posed**, for an audience with that view. It would show that **British opinion was not uniform**, though still a view from outside India.
